claims.text: The starting material is a laser-3D-printed CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a relatively coarse-grained microstructure.
A thin silver nanoparticle or silver nanocoating should be deposited on the CoCrFeNi surface before sliding.
The silver coating will form an Ag-rich, self-lubricating interfacial layer during sliding.
The Ag-rich interfacial layer will remain present from room temperature through 800 °C.
Frictional heating during sliding facilitates silver diffusion.
Tribo-chemical interactions cause silver particles to coalesce at the surface.
The Ag-containing lubricating film lowers interfacial shear strength.
The lubricating film reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
The lubricating film reduces plastic deformation during wear.
An Ag-containing TiNbZr alloy can form an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface layer during dry sliding.
The cited TiNbZr-Ag alloy exhibits a friction coefficient of about 0.09 in air at a maximum contact stress of 1.0 GPa.
Reactive formation of an oxidic nanocomposite surface reduced the wear rate of the cited TiNbZr-Ag alloy by an order of magnitude.
Ag-coated CoCrFeNi will have a lower and more stable friction coefficient than uncoated CoCrFeNi throughout room temperature to 800 °C.
Ag-coated CoCrFeNi will have a lower wear rate than uncoated CoCrFeNi throughout room temperature to 800 °C.
The proposed benefit will be especially strong at elevated temperatures because silver diffusion is enhanced.
Uncoated CoCrFeNi has higher friction and wear partly because of unstable oxide-film formation and plastic deformation under similar sliding conditions.
The hypothesis is limited to dry sliding in ambient air between room temperature and 800 °C, at loads of approximately 10–100 mN and typical tribological sliding speeds.

The hypothesis is falsified if coated samples show no statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate relative to uncoated controls, or if the Ag film fails to remain active throughout the temperature range.
